name: Foma
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

earlier_scan.note: Only wordlists (Stapleton, Johnston) and ethnography (Crine 1972); no phonological description exists.

new_statements.quote: b) Rhythmic patterns. In addition to tonal variations between an essentially high and an essentially low tone, the syllables of a word in speech can show differences in prominence which give the word a characteristic rhythm. In Kele and some surrounding languages the most prominent syllable in the spoken language is the penultimate, irrespective of the grammatical nature of this syllable. On the other hand, in some other Central African languages, e.g. Ngala (cf. 32, p. 8) the most prominent syllable is the initial syllable of the radical. [p.100:] ...the Foma tribe, a forest people whose spoken and gong-languages are almost identical with those of the riverine Lokele.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kele (Lokele) is a two-tone language (essentially high vs low syllable tones); independently of tone, the penultimate syllable of the word is the most prominent (rhythmic prominence), regardless of whether that syllable is prefix, radical or suffix -- explicitly contrasted with stem-initial prominence in Ngala. Carrington states (p.100) that Foma speech is almost identical with riverine Lokele, so the statement is taken to cover Foma.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned by Carrington. (Stapleton 1903:4, older and conflicting, gives main accent on the stem-initial syllable with 'a secondary and weaker accent' on the penult when more than two syllables follow.)
new_statements.exceptions: Carrington gives none. Conflicting earlier account: Stapleton 1903:4-5 sec. 8, written at Yakusu with Kele examples, puts the main accent on the initial syllable of the stem for 'the Congo languages', notes accent shift marking Neg. Imperative vs Subjunctive in Kele (owangéke / owángeke), and Swahili loans in Kele heard with penult accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word in connected speech ('the syllables of a word in speech.. the most prominent syllable in the spoken language'); Carrington separately describes clause-final and isolation-form pitch lowering ('final cadence', p.44) as a tonal, not prominence, effect. Statement is for Kele (Lokele) generally, Yakusu area; not elicited from Foma speakers specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: foma1238 is a retired Glottolog 'Bookkeeping' languoid (ISO fom Foma/Lifoma; Maho 2009 C56). Glottolog merges it into kele1255 'Kele-Foma' [khy] = Lokele, Guthrie C55 (Tshopo, Isangi/Yakusu area). First-hand sources agree the Foma speak Lokele: Carrington 1949:100 ('spoken and gong-languages.. almost identical with those of the riverine Lokele'); Motingea 2012:193 ('parlent aujourd'hui la même langue des Lokelé', citing Hulstaert 1950a:23, Van Bulck 1954:45; Bokula et al. 1979:20 'Bambole-Lokele'); Stapleton 1903 intro (Foma use Kele for trade); Johnston 1908:865 labels the Yakusu numerals 'Lokusu or Lofoma'. The quoted stress statement describes Kele (Lokele) generally, not speech elicited from Foma; no description of Foma speech itself exists beyond numerals/wordlists. Any catalog entry belongs under kele1255, not as a separate foma1238 record.

sources.note: pp.4-5 sec. 8 'On Accent': 'In the Congo languages the main accent falls on the initial syllable of the stem. When more than two syllables.. follow the accented syllable a secondary and weaker accent falls on the penult'; (c) accent shifted for grammatical distinction in Kele (owangéke 'fear not' vs owángeke); sec. 9 note: Swahili loans in Kele sometimes keep penult accent. Intro: Kele 'is used by the Turumbu, the Foma, and the Bakumu for trading purposes'. Conflicts with Carrington 1949 (penult prominence).
